title: The Slippery Case of the Truth
teaching_need: Learners can recite definitions of truth theories without being able to apply them when evidence conflicts, witnesses disagree, or a case changes underfoot—treating truth as a slogan rather than a disciplined judgement.
intended_capability: Form, test and revise a reasoned judgement about a contested case by applying competing accounts of truth, distinguishing evidence from interpretation, and defending a conclusion under uncertainty.
summary: A Learning Journey that opens with a contested case judgement, then develops philosophical tools—witnesses and records, correspondence and coherence, pragmatism and competing theories—before the case shifts and learners reconsider and defend their conclusion, supported by a Philosophical Learning Journal.
primary_pattern: Case-first philosophical judgement with progressive theoretical tools and mandatory reconsideration
supporting_patterns: Independent initial judgement before theoretical scaffolding
Progressive introduction of truth theories against a living case
Distinction between evidence, testimony, record and interpretation
Comparison of competing accounts of truth (including pragmatism)
Case change that forces revision rather than confirmation bias
Learning Journal preserving philosophical reasoning across the sequence
learning_sequence: Overview — orientation to the case and journey expectations
The case opens: Your first judgement — form an initial view before theory arrives
A witness, a record and a contradiction — weigh conflicting sources
What makes a claim true? — examine criteria for truth claims
Reality and coherence: Two accounts of truth — contrast correspondence and coherence
Pragmatism and the problem of competing theories — consider pragmatic tests and rivalry
The case changes: Evidence or interpretation? — confront a shifting evidentiary picture
Reconsidering your judgement — revise earlier conclusions in light of new tools and evidence
The philosophical case for your conclusion — defend a reasoned ending judgement
Philosophical Learning Journal — preserve and revisit learner-authored reasoning
transferable_principle: When learners can name theories without using them, begin with a contested case judgement, introduce theoretical tools only as they become necessary, then force reconsideration when the case or evidence changes—so theory serves judgement rather than replacing it. The crime-case framing is the vehicle; the case-first, reconsider-later logic travels.
